en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-Cuṇḍa-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Imperial Censor of the Third Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying in the country of Kauśāmbī, in the Ghoṣira Forest. At that time, there was a great elder named Cunda who came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he paid his respects by prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can these inexhaustible merits still be recovered?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Venerable Cunda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding his inexhaustible merits.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain them to you, Cunda!

This inexhaustible merit is profoundly subtle and its renown is heard everywhere; if one takes refuge in it with a devoted heart, one shall obtain a great fruit and retribution. Furthermore, this merit possesses seven aspects: its fame is universal, and it is profound and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family, having aroused a heart of utmost sincerity, is able to fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
What are the seven? "Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having developed great faith, give gardens, groves, and ponds for the monks of the four quarters to walk upon and dwell in."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the first inexhaustible merit, which yields great fruit and receives great praise; its renown is universal, profound, and vast."

If good sons or good daughters can fulfill this Dharma, such persons will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived great faith, establish a vihāra in that forest to provide a dwelling for the Saṃgha."
“Cunda! This is the second inexhaustible merit, which brings great fruit and reward, and even fame that is universally renowned, profound, and vast.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can fulfill this dharma, such a person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.”
"Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived great faith, bestow within the monasteries of that Saṃgha the requisites for sitting and reclining—namely:
beds, chairs, woolen rugs, mattresses, robes, coverlets, and various articles for use."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the third inexhaustible merit, which brings great fruit and reward, and whose renown is universally pervasive, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can, with a heart of utmost sincerity, fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived great faith, are able to bestow wealth and grain within that vihāra as an offering to the Saṃgha."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the fourth inexhaustible merit, which possesses great fruit and reward, and whose fame is universally pervasive, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can, with a sincere heart, fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived great faith, are able to constantly practice giving to the community of monks who come and go, providing them with all necessary requisites."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the fifth inexhaustible merit, which brings great fruit and reward, and even its renown is universally pervasive, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can develop a heart of sincere resolve and fully possess this dharma, that person will, within the four modes of conduct, constantly increase inexhaustible merit; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived great faith, are able to practice giving toward those suffering from illness, and also practice giving toward those who tend to the sick.
Kauṇḍinya! This is the sixth inexhaustible merit, which yields great fruit and reward, and whose renown is universal, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can, with a sincere heart, fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to great faith, and upon seeing hoarfrost, snow, freezing weather, wind, rain, or cold, they are able to prepare various kinds of food and drink, medicinal decoctions, bedding, clothing, shoes, and so forth, to provide and offer them to the community of monks."
In this way, the Sangha is not invaded by wind or rain and does not suffer from the cold; by receiving these offerings, they attain great peace and happiness.
Cunda! This is the seventh inexhaustible merit, which yields a great fruit and reward, and whose fame is even universal, profound, and vast.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having developed a heart of sincere resolve, is able to fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.

“Kunala! These seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious dharmas—if a son or daughter of good family should give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity and fulfill these dharmas—the inexhaustible merit they obtain will be inconceivable and immeasurable; such merit is exceedingly vast and is called a 'great mass of merit.'”
"Kauṇḍinya! It is, for example, like the five great rivers whose waters flow constantly:
namely, the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, the Aciravatī River, and the Mahī River."

Furthermore, this river water is immeasurable; such river water—even when contained in vessels numbering in the hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of billions—is so vast that it is called a "mass of water" (*āpa-skandha*).
Inexhaustible merit is likewise so!

“Kunala! When these seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious qualities are fully possessed, the merit obtained by those good sons and good daughters is inconceivable and immeasurable; they possess great renown and great retribution. Their merit is so vast that it is called a ‘great mass of merit.’”
At that time, the Great Elder Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding this inexhaustible merit—if a person is fully endowed with this Dharma, which is true and not false, they will obtain a great fruit and retribution, possess great renown, and their fame will be universal, profound, and vast?"
The Buddha addressed the Great Venerable Cunda, saying:
"As you have said, you have indeed attained these inexhaustible merits; such is the fruit of their retribution!
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Kunala! Furthermore, there are seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious dharmas that yield great rewards, possess great renown, and are universally celebrated, profound, and vast.”

If a son or daughter of good family, having aroused a heart of utmost sincerity, is able to fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
What are the seven? "Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear that the Tathāgata or the assembly of Śrāvakas are walking, wandering, or staying in a certain village or city, and having heard this, they give rise to great joy, cultivate a great wholesome intention, and resolve their minds upon Bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the first inexhaustible dharma of merit, which possesses great fruit and reward, is endowed with great renown, and is universally celebrated, profound, and vast."

If a son or daughter of good family is able to fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear of the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas—whether they have gone to a village or proceeded to a city—and having heard this, give rise to great joy, conceive a great wholesome intention, and resolve upon bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the second inexhaustible dharma of merit, which yields great fruit and reward, and whose renown is pervasive, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family with pure faith can fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of conduct; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear that the Tathāgata or the assembly of śrāvakas are on a journey, and having heard this, they give rise to great joy, cultivate a great wholesome intention, and resolve upon bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the third inexhaustible dharma of merit, which brings great fruit and reward, even unto the point that its fame becomes universally pervasive, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear that the Tathāgata or the assembly of Śrāvakas has arrived at a village or a city, and having heard this, they give rise to great joy, cultivate great wholesome intentions, and resolve upon Bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the fourth inexhaustible dharma of merit, which yields great fruit and even brings renown that is universal, profound, and vast.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of conduct; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear of the Tathāgata and his assembly of Śrāvakas—whether in a village or at a city gate—and go themselves to approach, pay homage to, and gaze upon them; having obtained the sight of them, they give rise to great joy, cultivate a great wholesome intention, and resolve their minds upon Bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the fifth inexhaustible dharma of merit, which yields great fruit and reward, and whose renown is far-reaching, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who go to the presence of the Buddha or to the presence of a Śrāvaka, prostrate and gaze upon them, and listen to the sublime Dharma; having heard this Dharma, they give rise to great joy, cultivate great wholesome intentions, and resolve their minds upon Bodhicitta."
"Kauṇḍinya! This is the sixth inexhaustible merit, which yields great fruit and reward, and whose fame is universally renowned, profound, and vast.

If a son or daughter of good family can fulfill this dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who, having heard this Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a śrāvaka, give rise to great wholesome intentions and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; and having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, they even receive the Tathāgata’s pure precepts."
Cunda! This is the seventh inexhaustible quality of merit, which yields great fruit and reward, and even brings renown that is universal, profound, and vast. Cunda!

If a son or daughter of good family, having aroused a heart of utmost sincerity, is able to fulfill this Dharma, that person will constantly increase inexhaustible merit within the four modes of deportment; the merit thus increased is inconceivable and immeasurable.
"Kunala! If any son or daughter of good family is able to fulfill these seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious dharmas, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable."

Kauṇḍinya! These seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious dharmas—if there be sons or daughters of good family who, having resolved with a sincere heart, can fully possess these dharmas, the inexhaustible merit they obtain shall be immeasurable.
Such merit, renown, praise, and the merit of great karmic fruition are so vast that they are called a "great aggregate of merit.
Furthermore, Cunda:
It is like five great rivers that flow with water constantly:
namely, the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, the Aciravatī River, and the Mahī River.

Furthermore, this river water is immeasurable; such river water—even when contained in vessels numbering in the hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of billions—is so vast that it is called a "mass of water" (*āpa-skandha*).
Inexhaustible merit is likewise so!

"Kunala! These seven kinds of inexhaustible meritorious qualities are all fully possessed by these good sons and good daughters; the merit they obtain is inconceivable and immeasurable. They possess great renown and great retribution; their merit is so vast that it is called a 'great mass of merit'."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Purify your cultivation of dhyāna; Cultivate only within the traces of the Noble Ones.
In gathering jewels, none surpasses the ocean; Like a river, ferry sentient beings across."
"The waters of the river have no bound; / All streams return to their source.
/ Through giving one obtains great merit, / Like a river that flows constantly to the sea.
At that time, the Great Venerable Cunda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, paid homage, and accepted it with faith to put into practice.
The Sūtra on Cunda Spoken by the Buddha
